subject: mathematics
question_text: Using the principle of finite Mathematical Induction prove that 1² + (1² + 2²) + (1² + 2² + 3²) + … n terms = n(n+1)²(n+2)/12, ∀ n ∈ N.

mark_split.label: nth term and the statement S(n)

verification.note: Source: Baby Bullet-Q, Junior Inter Maths-1A (Sri Publishers, Machilipatnam), book p.17 — LAQ chapter 2, question 6. The 1+1+1+3+1 split is PRINTED in that book's margin. Publisher's claims until a Telangana IPE teacher confirms them. Re-cut to the 8-mark Section-C form of the 2026-27 pattern (TGBIE model paper w.e.f. 2026-27): the extra mark goes to Step 3 — S(k+1) follows.

recall_prompt: Say how you would prove this by induction — what the nth term is, and how the third step finishes.

steps.label: Find the nth term
steps.margin_note: One mark. Each term is itself a sum of squares, so the nth term needs the standard sum-of-squares formula before S(n) can be written.

recall.must_convey: That the nth term is itself the sum of the first n squares, n(n+1)(2n+1)/6, and that S(n) is then written in full.
accept: each term is the sum of squares so the nth term is n into n plus one into two n plus one over six
use the standard sum of squares formula for the general term
the nth term is the sum of the first n squares which is n n plus one two n plus one by six
sum of squares formula vaadi nth term rastam

steps.why: The terms are nested sums, so the nth term is a formula rather than a product. Getting it wrong makes every later line wrong.
common_mistakes: Using n² as the nth term instead of the SUM of squares up to n.
Misremembering the sum of squares as n(n+1)/2, which is the sum of the first n numbers.

steps.label: Check S(1)
steps.margin_note: One mark. Both sides at n = 1 come to 1.
lines: ∴ L.H.S = R.H.S, so S(1) is true.

recall.must_convey: That at n = 1 the left side is 1² = 1 and the right side is 1(2)²(3)/12 = 1, so S(1) holds.
accept: left side is one squared which is one and right side is one into two squared into three over twelve which is one
both sides give one at n equals one
twelve over twelve is one so the first case is true
n equals one ki rendu sides one vasthai

steps.why: The base case is cheap here but it is a full mark, and without it the chain has no first link.
common_mistakes: Skipping the arithmetic and writing 'clearly true'.
Substituting into the nth-term formula instead of the statement.

steps.label: Assume S(k) is true
steps.margin_note: One mark. Assume the statement for one value k and NUMBER the line (1) — Step 3 quotes it, so it has to be labelled.
lines: Step 2 — assume S(k) is true, k ∈ N

recall.must_convey: That S(k) is ASSUMED true for some k in N, written out as the sum up to k terms equals k(k+1)²(k+2)/12, and labelled (1) for later use.
accept: assume the statement is true for k so the sum up to k terms equals k(k+1)²(k+2)/12
suppose s of k holds and call it equation one
take it as true for some k in the naturals and number that line
k ki true ani assume chesi equation one ga rastam
reject: then I assume s of k
let it be true for k

steps.why: This is the assumption the whole method rests on. It is not proved here — it is granted for ONE value, and Step 3 earns the right to pass it on.
common_mistakes: Assuming the statement for ALL k, which assumes what is being proved.
Not numbering the line, so Step 3 cannot cite it.

steps.label: Show S(k+1) follows
steps.margin_note: Four marks. Write the (k+1)th term first, add it to (1), put everything over 12, then factorise out (k+1)(k+2).
lines: So S(k+1) is true whenever S(k) is true.

recall.must_convey: That the (k+1)th term is (k+1)(k+2)(2k+3)/6, that both fractions go over 12, and that factoring out (k+1)(k+2) leaves k² + 5k + 6 = (k+2)(k+3), giving (k+1)(k+2)²(k+3)/12.
accept: the next term is k plus one k plus two two k plus three over six then take everything over twelve and factor out k plus one k plus two
the bracket becomes k squared plus five k plus six which factors as k plus two into k plus three
after factorising you get k plus one into k plus two squared into k plus three over twelve
common factor teeste k square plus five k plus six vasthundi adi k plus two k plus three
heard_as: k squared plus five k plus six

steps.why: The quadratic k² + 5k + 6 factorising as (k+2)(k+3) is the moment the answer appears — the second (k+2) is what makes the square in the formula.
common_mistakes: Getting the (k+1)th term wrong: replace n by k+1 in n(n+1)(2n+1)/6, which gives 2k+3, not 2k+1.
Failing to bring both fractions to the same denominator before adding.
Leaving k² + 5k + 6 unfactorised, so R.H.S never appears.

steps.label: Conclude by P.M.I
steps.margin_note: The last mark is for naming the principle. Write the sentence — it is one line and it is worth a full mark.
lines: Hence, by the principle of finite

recall.must_convey: That because S(1) is true AND S(k) implies S(k+1), the principle of mathematical induction gives the result for every natural number n.
accept: since s of one is true and s of k implies s of k plus one by the principle of mathematical induction it is true for all n
hence by p m i the statement holds for every natural number
the base case and the inductive step together give it for all n in n
p m i prakaram anni natural numbers ki true

steps.why: The two earlier parts prove single statements. Only the principle turns them into a claim about every n, so the examiner marks the sentence that names it.
common_mistakes: Writing only 'hence proved' and never naming the principle.
Claiming it for all real numbers instead of all n ∈ N.
